### 2026-07-04 — Premiärer & finaler (premieres.ts): DST guard that doesn't guard
A DST window test is only a real regression guard when the *buggy* fixed-ms path
would produce a DIFFERENT calendar date than the setDate stride (same lesson as
BIN-105's "would have been index 0 under the old fixed-ms approach"). `quarterWindow`'s
spring test (`new Date(2026,2,20)` → endIso `2026-06-19`) FAILS this bar: because the
start is normalized to local midnight and spring-forward only *adds* an hour
(00:00→01:00), a fixed-ms `start.getTime()+91*86400000` yields the SAME date. Verified:
setDate==ms for the spring anchor. The window that would catch a fixed-ms revert crosses
the FALL-BACK transition (gain 1h pushes midnight+Nd back to 23:00 the prior day): anchor
`2026-07-27` → setDate `2026-10-26` vs ms `2026-10-25`. **Rule for review:** when a test's
comment claims "a fixed-ms diff would drift," mentally run the buggy impl at that fixture —
if it lands on the same asserted value, the test proves the day-COUNT (91 vs 90) but NOT
DST-safety, and should either move to a fall-back anchor or add one. The rest of the suite
is honest: K2 disjoint counting (premiereFinales subtraction) pinned in copy.test.ts;
live-beats-pill dedupe via entryKey pinned; E1-only premiere pills + 5-way rejection each
independently fail the combined length-0 assertion; sv-collation sort (Ö last) real;
discovery cap/cross-page-dedupe/exclusion/getDisplayTitle all covered. No weakened/skipped
assertions.

CORRECTION APPLIED + verified. A "91 calendar days DST-safe" test only guards the

fall-back (clocks GAIN an hour → fixed-ms lands 1h short → prior local day). Spring-forward
never crosses a midnight boundary, so buggy and correct impls agree → tautological green.

fixed-ms would fail it. LESSON: any DST-safety date test must anchor so the tested span
crosses a *fall-back* — assert exact ISO, and prove the buggy impl yields a different value.

### 2026-07-05 (same day, third pass) — BIN-184 xhigh fix: flipped rules expectation is a legitimate strengthening, not a weakening

An xhigh-workflow security pass found a real GDPR blocker: the household rules' single
`allow read` required share-to-see reciprocity (membership + an own contribution doc) even
for a member reading their OWN doc via GET. Two production flows broke: (a) `buildUserExport`
calling `getDoc` on the user's own `groups/{gid}/household/{uid}` for every group membership
— denied outright for a non-opted-in member/owner, crashing the whole export; (b)
`collectDeletionRefs`'s owner branch, which used to `getDocs(collection(...,'household'))` (a
LIST query) to enumerate all contributions for full-group erasure — LIST also required the
owner's own share-to-see reciprocity, so an owner who never opted into their own group's
household silently broke account deletion. Both are real, previously-masked bugs — not
theoretical.

**The fix, verified in `firestore.rules`:** the single `allow read` was split into `allow get`
(self-uid always allowed regardless of membership/opt-in/departure, exists()=false is a valid
non-denied outcome; OTHERS' docs still need share-to-see) and `allow list` (unchanged strict
share-to-see reciprocity — a non-sharing member still cannot browse the full collection).
This preserves the privacy property (LIST is still gated) while fixing the two flows (both use
GET on known ids, never LIST for their own membership). `collectDeletionRefs`'s owner branch
was rewritten to derive household refs from the already-fetched `membersSnap` member ids
(`householdUids`) plus self, rather than a LIST query — `batch.delete` on a non-existent doc
ref is a no-op, so pushing a ref per member is safe and side-steps the LIST-permission problem
entirely.

**Test changes assessed as a genuine strengthening, verified against the rule text and
production code directly (not just re-reading test prose):**
1. `firestore-rules.test.ts` "departed member" test FLIPPED from assertFails-on-own-doc to
   assertSucceeds-on-own-doc — traced against the new split rule: self-GET has no membership
   clause at all (`request.auth.uid == householdUid` is the whole first disjunct), so a
   departed member's own stale doc is genuinely still gettable. OTHERS' docs are untouched —
   the same test still asserts `assertFails` on getting the OWNER's doc as a departed member,
   preserving the reciprocity guard for non-self reads. Two new tests (own-missing-doc GET
   succeeds; LIST still denies a non-sharing member and succeeds for a sharing one) each map
   to one new/preserved clause in the rule. Household describe block count: 13 → 15,
   confirmed by direct grep count. Total emulator suite 142 → 144, arithmetic checks out
   (+2, nothing removed).
2. `account-deletion.test.ts`: `mygroup`'s `memberUids` gained `OTHER`, a `members/{OTHER}`
   doc was added, and — deliberately — ME's (the owner's) own household doc was DROPPED from
   the seed (previously both ME's and OTHER's docs existed). This is not an assertion weakened
   to fit buggy output; it's a seed change that exercises the exact bug class the xhigh pass
   found (an owner who never opted in). Confirmed by reading `accountDeletion.ts` directly:
   the owner branch now derives `householdUids` from `membersSnap.docs.map(id)` + `add(id)`
   unconditionally — self is always included in the erasure set regardless of whether a
   self-doc exists, so the mechanism that deletes OTHER's doc is identical to the one that
   would delete ME's if it existed. `expect(count(...,'household'))===0` remains a genuine
   two-sided oracle for the new seed: only OTHER's doc exists pre-deletion, so 0 specifically
   proves OTHER's doc — the one doc that could reveal a LIST-permission regression — is gone.
   This directly answers the "is OTHER's doc erasure still covered" question: yes.
   `othergroup` (member-leaves branch) assertions are untouched byte-for-byte.
3. `dataExport.coverage.test.ts` source-grep: `householdSnap` (old list-query destructure
   variable, which no longer exists anywhere in `accountDeletion.ts` post-refactor) replaced
   with `householdUids` (the new variable name), with an inline comment explaining the "why."
   Verified by reading the production file directly — `householdUids` appears exactly once,
   in the owner branch, and would fail to match if that branch reverted to a list-query
   variable name. Not a wording-only rename to dodge a real gap; the underlying mechanism
   genuinely changed and the grep target changed with it.

**One minor, non-blocking observation (not the coordinator's flagged item, found independently):**
the `dataExport.coverage.test.ts` comment above the source-grep still reads "owner branch
enumerates the household collection" — this phrasing is now stale (it derives from member ids,
it no longer enumerates via a collection query). Purely a comment/prose staleness, no assertion
is affected; worth a one-line fix next time this test is touched, not blocking.

**One minor, non-blocking gap (same class as the "no test owed" acceptable-gap precedent):**
the new `account-deletion.test.ts` seed no longer has a fixture proving "the owner's OWN
household doc, if it exists, is included in the full-collection erasure" (the old seed did,
via count===0 with both docs present; the new seed deliberately omits ME's doc to test the
opposite, more valuable case). This is provably covered by code inspection (`householdUids
.add(id)` unconditionally, no branch distinguishes self from other members in the ref-push
loop) rather than by a redundant seed fixture — acceptable, but a future "belt-and-suspenders"
addition would be a THIRD group fixture: owner opted in AND another member opted in, asserting
both erased. Not required before shipping; the mechanism is structurally identical for self vs.
other member ids, so there's no plausible code path that would pass the current test while
failing this untested one.

**Verdict: APPROVED.** The flipped expectation + seed change is a legitimate strengthening that
closes a previously-masked GDPR-blocking bug, not a weakening. No assertion was loosened to
match buggy output — the rule and the code both genuinely changed, and the tests changed in
lockstep with a clear paper trail (inline comments citing the xhigh review) explaining why.

  `existingCoverage:'none'` × `wouldBeCoverage:'none'` combos:
  `seasonUploadDecision({missingCount:8,episodeCount:8,seasonOnlyFlag:true,existingCoverage:'full',force:true})`
  → `{ allow: true, coverage: 'none', upgraded: false }`. **This is a real, silent full→none
  downgrade path: `--force --season-only` on a show that already has a full per-episode-covered
  season doc overwrites it with a lower-fidelity season-only doc, with `upgraded:false` (no
  distinct signal) — the exact mirror of the `none→full` path, which DOES get its own refusal
  message without `--force` and its own `upgraded:true` flag on write. No test exercises
  `existingCoverage:'full'` with `wouldBeCoverage:'none'` at all (either force value).** The test
  named for this scenario — `'a full→none "downgrade" never happens — full coverage always wins
  over the season-only flag'` — actually uses `existingCoverage: null` (no existing doc in the
  fixture at all), so it tests something different and narrower (that `missingCount===0`
  short-circuits to `'full'` ahead of the `seasonOnlyFlag` check in the ternary) — a real, useful
  guard, but its name promises the existing-doc downgrade scenario it doesn't touch. **Report
  distinctly to the ticket owner** (script-safety/UX gap, low exploit risk — internal ops CLI
  requiring both `--force` and `--season-only` — but the asymmetry with the upgrade path's named
  reason + flag looks like an oversight, not a deliberate design call; not listed in
  accepted-deviations.md).
- **Lesson for the reviewer role: when a test's `it()` name states an X-vs-Y claim
  ("not every prior season", "downgrade never happens"), verify the ARGUMENTS actually construct
  the X-vs-Y contrast, not just that the assertion is true** — both gaps above are cases where the
  assertion holds, the test passes, and the code may even be correct, but the fixture doesn't
  isolate the specific mechanism the name claims to guard. Cheap to verify: hand-run the pure
  function (or live-mutate the component) with the SPECIFIC alternate implementation the name
  implies and check the existing suite still passes before trusting the name.

### 2026-07-18 — BIN-523/529 availableNotify re-attempt (post 2026-07-16 revert): collision fix genuinely test-locked, key-function-only tests are sufficient BECAUSE the wiring uses the tested keys verbatim

**Context:** first review of this exact diff (BIN-523's revert on 2026-07-16 is a different, earlier
version of this ticket — see that entry above). New: `normalizeMediaType`/`availableStateDocId`/
`inboxNotifId` in `functions/src/availableNotify/logic.ts` + 3 new describe blocks in
`logic.test.ts`, purely additive (`git diff` shows only new `import`s + new blocks, zero touched
assertions). Task explicitly asked whether a test proves the movie/TV tmdbId-collision scenario is
fixed, not just that the helpers "run".

**Answer: yes, and mutation-tested to confirm it's not decorative.** Live-mutated the real
`availableStateDocId` in `logic.ts` to ignore `mediaType` (`return \`${tmdbId}\`` — reintroducing
the exact pre-fix collision) → ran the suite → exactly 3 tests failed (`movie N vs tv N distinct
state ids`, `blank/unknown mediaType→tv fallback`, `movie N vs tv N distinct inbox ids`), 14/17
stayed green including the "rides availableStateDocId" lockstep test (correctly tautological — it
computes its expectation via the same function, so it can't catch a bug IN that function, only a
drift BETWEEN the two functions). Restored from a scratchpad backup, `diff` byte-identical.

**Why key-function-only tests were sufficient here (not a gap):** traced `index.ts`'s wiring by
hand — the Map that used to be `Map<number, WatchlistTitleLite[]>` keyed on bare `tmdbId` is now
`Map<string, ...>` keyed literally on `availableStateDocId(it.mediaType, it.tmdbId)` (not a
re-derived or approximated key), and the per-user inbox doc id is literally
`inboxNotifId(mediaType, tmdbId, providerId)` (not string-templated separately). Because the
grouping/dedup loop itself lives inline in `onSchedule(...)` (admin-import, can't run under root
vitest — the test file's own comment says so explicitly), there's no pure `groupByStateId()` to
extract and test directly; but since production literally calls the tested function AS the map key
with no intermediate logic, proving the function is injective-per-(mediaType,tmdbId) is
mathematically equivalent to proving the grouping is collision-free. This matches the established
"extract the pure helper, leave the wiring uncovered" convention (2026-07-09 BIN-440, 2026-07-16
revert entry, 2026-07-17 BIN-541 entry) — flagged for visibility, not a blocker, same as those.

**Verdict: APPROVED.** No weakened/deleted/skipped assertions; 17/17 pass; `firestore.rules`'s
concurrently-pending diff (unrelated `M firestore.rules` in `git status`) has zero overlap with
`availableNotify` (grep for `availableNotify`/`notification` in the rules diff: no hits) —
`availableNotifyState` is server-only via admin SDK, never touched by client rules, so no
rules-test update was owed for this ticket.

**Pattern reinforced:** when a reviewer is asked "does a test prove a collision scenario is fixed,
not just that a function returns a plausible string" — the discriminator isn't whether the test
constructs full domain objects (`WatchlistTitleLite`) or just calls the key function with raw args;
it's whether production code consumes the tested function's OUTPUT as the actual dedup/grouping
key with no re-derivation in between. Confirm that by reading the consumer, then mutation-test the
key function itself (cheaper and more direct than trying to mutate-test an untestable inline loop).

### 2026-07-15 — BIN-505 re-verify: gap 1 genuinely closed, gap 3+4 genuinely closed
(emulator/unit-run confirmed), but gap 2's REWRITE did not fix the underlying bug — it's
the same accidental-pass, just relocated, and mutation-testing proves it

**Context:** re-reviewed the BIN-505 test surface after a round of fixes claiming to close
3 previously flagged gaps. Ran everything for real rather than trusting the diff/claims.

**Gap 1 (missing `publicProfile.ts` tests) — CLOSED, genuinely discriminating.** New
`src/lib/firebase/publicProfile.test.ts` keys its `fsdb()` mock's `doc()`/`getDoc` DIRECTLY
in the mock factory (no dynamic `import('firebase/firestore')` inside it) — this sidesteps
the race described in gap 2 entirely (see below) and is the pattern to recommend when
fixing gap 2. Covers missing/denied/readable, batch omit-unreadable, signature-skip +
re-write-on-change, and explicitly asserts sensitive fields (`email`/`providerCosts`/
`hemkommun`) never appear in the projection payload. Re-ran 5× — stable.

**Gap 2 (`userSearch.test.ts` accidental-pass) — STILL OPEN, not closed by the rewrite.**
The rewrite is a real improvement in *intent* (keys the mock on doc PATH instead of call
order, adds legit self-exclusion + missing-projection tests that don't touch the bug).
But the one test that matters — "utesluter en profil vars projektion inte är läsbar och
tar med den läsbara" (2 concurrent candidates, one denied one readable) — still uses the
`fsdb: async () => ({ ...(await import('firebase/firestore')), db: {} })` pattern, and
`searchUsersByPrefix` fans out via `Promise.all(matches.map(getPublicProfileCard))`.
**Proved by mutation-testing** (scratch copy, deleted after): instrumented `getDocMock` to
record every `ref._path` it actually received — of 3 total `fsdb()` calls in one run (1 for
the `getDocs` username query + 2 for the two concurrent `getPublicProfileCard` calls), one
of the two `getPublicProfileCard` calls consistently resolved a real, UNMOCKED
`firebase/firestore` module (confirmed via `getDoc.toString()` showing the real function
body) instead of the mock — every single time across 40 iterations, not a rare flake. Then
changed the mock to make BOTH candidates readable (the mutation that should make the test
assert `length === 2`) and the harness still returned only 1 result, 15/15 iterations —
proof the exclusion isn't coming from the simulated `Missing or insufficient permissions`
throw at all; it's coming from the real getDoc crashing on a fake `{_path}` ref object,
unconditionally killing whichever concurrent branch loses the race. The test would pass
identically whether `searchUsersByPrefix`'s visibility gate were correct, inverted, or
deleted. **Fix: don't test the concurrent 2-candidate scenario at all — split it into two
single-candidate tests** (matching the already-correct pattern used for the
missing-projection and self-exclusion cases in the same file), or switch the mock to the
`publicProfile.test.ts` style (inline functions in the `fsdb()` factory, no dynamic
`import('firebase/firestore')`) so there's nothing to race.

**Gap 3 (deletion-cascade emulator test) — CLOSED, emulator-verified.** Traced
`accountDeletion.ts` line-by-line: `watchlistNotesSnap.docs.forEach(d => refs.push(d.ref))`
and `refs.push(snaps.publicProfileSnap.ref)` are real, not just referenced in a coverage
map. Ran `npm run test:rules` live (Java 21, Firestore emulator) → 173/173 green, including
the new `publicProfiles/{ME}` + `watchlistNotes/603` erasure assertions.

**Gap 4 (`addItem` notes-strip) — CLOSED, genuinely locks the fix.** Traced
`WatchlistContext.tsx`'s `addItem`: destructures `const { notes: _strippedNotes,
...itemFields } = item;` before the `setDoc` call — structurally can't leak `notes` into
the watchlist-doc write regardless of caller. The new test asserts `'notes' in call![1]`
is `false`, which would fail if that destructure were ever reverted.

**Full re-run:** 1908/1908 unit + 173/173 rules, both executed live in this review (not
trusted from the task description).

**Lesson (generalizes the 2026-07-15 BIN-505 entry above): a "path-keyed instead of
order-keyed mock" fix does NOT close a `Promise.all`-concurrency mock-race bug — the race
is in module resolution (which `getDoc` implementation a given call binds to), not in which
mock branch answers which uid. Re-keying the assertion logic is orthogonal to the actual
bug. When this class of bug is flagged, verify the fix by mutation-testing (force the
"wrong" answer into the mock and confirm the test now fails) rather than re-reading the
diff — a green re-run after a well-intentioned refactor is not evidence the underlying
race is gone.**

**2026-07-15 (same day) follow-up — gap 2 CLOSED for real.** Coordinator applied the exact
fix recommended above: `userSearch.test.ts`'s `fsdb()` mock rewritten to return INLINE
functions (`getDoc: getDocMock`, `query: queryMock`, `where: whereMock`, plain object
literals for `doc`/`collection`/`limit`/`orderBy`/`documentId`) — no `vi.mock('firebase/
firestore', ...)`, no dynamic `import()` anywhere in the mock factory, matching
`publicProfile.test.ts`'s already-safe pattern. Independently re-verified (not just trusted
the coordinator's own mutation-test claim): ran the normal suite 5× (7/7 stable), then wrote
a fresh, separate mutation probe (scratch file, deleted after) covering BOTH falsifiable
directions — forced both candidates "readable" (should include both, and recorded which
`_path`s the mock actually received to rule out a silent bypass) and forced both "denied"
(should exclude both) — 40/40 iterations correct in both directions, both `getDoc` calls
provably reaching the mock every time. The gate is now genuinely exercised. All 4 BIN-505
gaps from this review cycle are closed. Full re-run: 1908/1908 unit + typecheck clean
(rules suite unchanged by this fix, not re-run this pass).

### 2026-07-09 — BIN-439 selectBundleSuggestions extraction: clean mechanical extract-then-test, no weakening

**Context:** `useSubscriptionAdvisor.ts`'s inline `enabled ? detectBundleArbitrage(...) : []`
ternary (flagged as untested hook-wiring in the 2026-07-07 BIN-430 entry above) is now
pulled into `selectBundleSuggestions(enabled, ownedProviderIds, costSettings, bundles, now,
detect=detectBundleArbitrage)` in `useSubscriptionAdvisor.helpers.ts`, with an injectable
`detect` param (default = real engine) for test-only substitution. The hook call site is a
byte-for-byte behavior-preserving swap (same 4 real args, same `useMemo` deps array,
unchanged). Confirmed via `tsc --noEmit`, `eslint`, and `vitest run` (54/54 green) — no
regressions, no `any`.

**Four new tests in `useSubscriptionAdvisor.test.ts`, all genuine oracles:**
1. `enabled=false` → `[]` AND `detect` not called — proper gate + no-call assertion (not just
   the return value).
2. `enabled=true` → `toHaveBeenCalledWith(OWNED, SETTINGS, SWEDISH_BUNDLES, NOW)` — pins ALL
   four forwarded args in one assertion, not just arity.
3. `enabled=true` → `toBe(sentinel)` (identity, not `toEqual`) — proves no post-processing/
   copy of the engine's return value.
4. Default-param test: calls `selectBundleSuggestions(true, ..., SWEDISH_BUNDLES, NOW)` (no
   `detect` override) and asserts `.toEqual(detectBundleArbitrage(...))` called directly on
   the same args — proves the default parameter genuinely resolves to the real production
   function, not a stub. **Notably avoids the BIN-403 price-agent catalog-coupling trap**
   (see `project_price_agent_test_coupling` memory): rather than hardcoding an expected
   `BundleSuggestion[]` shape (which would break every time `SWEDISH_BUNDLES` catalog data
   changes), it computes the expected value by calling the real engine on the SAME inputs —
   both sides move together if the catalog changes, so this assertion is catalog-price-change-
   immune while still being a genuine (non-tautological) proof of correct default-wiring.

**No assertion touched, no `.skip`/`.only`, no weakening.** Verdict: PASS, no gaps found.
**Pattern to keep:** when pinning that a default parameter equals a real production function
(not a stub), prefer "call the real function directly on the same inputs and compare" over
hardcoding expected output — it's both a stronger oracle (catches accidental default-swaps)
and immune to catalog/fixture-data drift.

### 2026-07-09 — BIN-440 traceability recovery: the LOST BIN-430 medium production concern is the resilience-claim-vs-consumer-guard mismatch (re-derived + graded REAL)

**Context:** BIN-430's test-reviewer marker header promised "one medium production-code
correctness concern" in the bundle-suggestions wiring but the marker body never wrote it
down (it re-expanded a BIN-433 entry instead). BIN-439 recovered the *test* gap; this
re-derives the lost *production* concern. Already-cleared candidate (do not re-report):
raw `myProviders` vs `canonMyProviders` fed to the engine — safe, engine canonicalizes at
`bundleArbitrage.ts:246`.

**The concern (REAL, medium): a hook-level resilience CLAIM defeated at its only consumer.**
`useSubscriptionAdvisor.ts:489-493` documents `bundleSuggestions` as computed independently
of the TMDB fan-out so it "överlever ett TMDB-fel" (survives a TMDB error) — TRUE at the hook
(the memo reads only `myProviders`+cost settings; `return {...computed, bundleSuggestions}` at
:506 adds it after the spread so `computed`'s error-path shape can't clobber it). But the SOLE
consumer `savings/page.tsx:200` early-returns the generic `<EmptyState "Inga tjänster tillagda
än">` whenever `advisor.providers.length === 0`, and `<BundleArbitrageCard>` sits at :259
*after* that guard. `computed` sets `providers: []` in exactly the total-outage branch
(`hasError && shows.length === 0`, :136-149). Concrete trigger: enabled (savings page always),
user has ≥1 followed/vill_se TV (queries exist), every `tv-lite` query errors with no cached
data (cold-cache TMDB outage), AND ≥2 paid bundle-eligible owned services → `bundleSuggestions`
correctly non-empty, yet the page renders "no services added" and hides the card the comment
promised would still show. Narrow trigger (total outage + cold cache) → medium, non-blocking.
Fix: render the card independent of / above the `providers.length===0` guard (or gate on
`bundleSuggestions.length > 0`), ideally behind a real TMDB-error state rather than the
misleading empty-state. Regression test owed: render `SavingsContent` with advisor stubbed to
`{providers:[], isLoading:false, hasError:true, bundleSuggestions:[oneSuggestion]}` and assert
the card is present — none exists today (no `savings/page.tsx` test at all, consistent with the
rest of `src/app/savings/`, which is WHY the marker claim went unverified).

**Pattern (reinforces the 2026-07-07 BIN-430 entry): a code COMMENT asserting a resilience/
independence property is a claim a reviewer must try to break at the CONSUMER, not just the
producer. When a derived value is deliberately built to survive failure mode X, trace every
consumer's render guards — if any routes through X's own early return before reaching the
value, the property is real but unobservable, and there's usually no test because the
producer is unit-tested in isolation while the consumer page is not.** Second-order lesson for
marker hygiene: a marker HEADER that promises "N notes below" must be diffed against the BODY —
an unwritten promised finding is a traceability defect in its own right (this whole ticket).

### 2026-07-09 — BIN-423 WP3 prunePersonSeed: PASS-WITH-NOTES — a "drops fat fields" test that only pins TWO of the dropped fields doesn't prove the byte-reduction contract

**Context:** `prunePersonSeed(person)` trims a TMDB person's appended `combined_credits`
to only the fields the person-page filmography renders, caps cast to top-200 by
`vote_average`, passes an old-shape person (no `combined_credits`) through unchanged. New
test file `src/lib/tmdb/personSeed.test.ts`, no Firebase import, correct for root vitest.
All net-new — no `.skip`/`.only`, no weakened assertion, strict matchers throughout.

**Verified-honest oracles:**
- Cap test is genuine: 250 credits built in ASCENDING vote_average (0..249) — input differs
  from the descending output so the `.sort` is actually exercised — then `min(kept)===50`
  proves the RIGHT 200 (highest) survived, not merely `length===200`. This is the correct
  "prove selection, not just count" pattern (contrast the BIN-110 6-vs-15000 vacuous cap).
- `as unknown as TMDBSearchResult` malformed-credit test is LEGITIMATE, not a type-issue
  mask: `pruneCredit` deliberately has `vote_average ?? 0` / `genre_ids ?? []` because real
  TMDB rows drop these and `TitleCard` calls `vote_average.toFixed(1)`. Constructing an
  off-type runtime shape is the honest way to exercise the `??` defaults; asserting only the
  two defaulted fields is correctly targeted.
- Identity passthrough (`toBe(p)`), character preservation, crew `job` preservation all pinned.

**Gap 1 (MEDIUM, the important one) — the byte-reduction contract is NOT pinned.** The whole
purpose of the helper is dropping the fat fields (`vote_count`, `popularity`, `credit_id`,
`episode_count`, `original_language`, …) that `pruneCredit` omits by explicit-field allowlist.
The "drops fat fields" test only asserts `overview===''` and `backdrop_path===null`. A
regression to `return { ...c, overview:'', backdrop_path:null }` (spread instead of allowlist)
would re-leak EVERY heavy field and re-bloat the ~1000 static /person pages — and every current
assertion would still pass. The fixture already carries `vote_count: 1000`, so pin the drop
directly: `expect('vote_count' in c).toBe(false)` (and ideally `popularity`/`credit_id`). Use
key-absence (`'x' in c`), not value checks. **Pattern: for an allowlist-prune helper whose
value proposition is SHRINKAGE, at least one dropped field the fixture actually sets must be
asserted absent — otherwise a spread-instead-of-allowlist regression is invisible.**

**Gap 2 (MEDIUM) — three consumed passthrough fields are untested: `name`, `original_name`,
`first_air_date`.** Confirmed consumed in `client.ts`: `getDisplayTitle` uses `title||name`
+ `original_title||original_name` (:321-322), `getReleaseYear` uses `release_date||first_air_date`
(:331). The single kept-fields fixture is a MOVIE with `name:undefined`/`original_name:undefined`
and no `first_air_date`, so a TV credit's display-title + year (which come ENTIRELY from those
three fields) are never pinned — dropping any of them from `pruneCredit`'s allowlist would slip
through. Add a `media_type:'tv'` credit fixture asserting `name`/`original_name`/`first_air_date`
survive. **Pattern: a `X||Y` fallback field-pair (localized-or-original title, release-or-air
date) needs a fixture exercising the Y branch — a movie-only fixture only proves the X side.**

**Minor:** crew is deliberately NOT capped (design comment says so, to not drop a directed film
from the meter) — no test pins "250 crew stay 250"; the `cc.cast ?? []` / `cc.crew ?? []` nullish
guards (subcollection present but arrays absent) are untested. Both low severity.

**Update 2026-07-09 (re-run) — both MEDIUM gaps CLOSED, verified honest.** Author added: (1)
`expect('vote_count' in c).toBe(false)` inside the kept-fields test — the fixture sets
`vote_count: 1000`, and `pruneCredit` builds by explicit allowlist (no `vote_count` key), so the
key-absence oracle is discriminating: a `{ ...c, overview:'', backdrop_path:null }` spread
regression re-adds vote_count → `'vote_count' in c` becomes true → fails. One pinned dropped
field carries the whole spread-vs-allowlist regression class (any spread re-leaks ALL fat
fields), so not also pinning popularity/credit_id is fine — they aren't in the fixture and
adding them would prove nothing extra. (2) New test "preserves TV display fields" — a
`media_type:'tv'` credit with title/original_title/release_date `undefined` and
name/original_name/first_air_date set, asserting all three survive; matches `pruneCredit`'s
allowlist lines (`name`/`original_name`/`first_air_date` all forwarded). Exercises the Y branch
of both `X||Y` fallbacks that the movie-only fixture left unpinned. Neither assertion is
tautological; no existing assertion touched, no `.skip`/`.only`. 6/6 green. Verdict: PASS.

above). A high-effort `/code-review` found the `vote_average` top-200 cap made truncation
USER-visible (person page reuses the build-seed and skips the full `/combined_credits` fetch,
so capped rows are simply gone from the UI — and vote_average-sort drops the newest un-voted
titles, exactly what a visitor looks for). Production fix REMOVED the cap: `prunePersonSeed`
now `.map`s cast/crew field-pruning-only, no `.slice`/`.sort` (confirmed by reading
`personSeed.ts` — the OBS comment lines 21-28 documents the removal). Both prod + test staged
net-new (whole WP3 lands fresh; the earlier PASS was against a working-tree draft).

**The one changed test — REPLACEMENT verified honest, not a red flag:**
- OLD: "caps cast to top 200 by vote_average, dropping the low-rated tail" (250 asc input →
  `length===200`, `min(kept)===50` proved the RIGHT 200 survived — a genuine sort+select oracle
  at the time).
- NEW: "keeps every cast row — prunes fields, never drops credits" (250 input → `length===250`).
- **This is the correct direction:** production behavior changed via review, the test follows to
  pin the CORRECTED contract. Keeping the old cap test would now FAIL against fixed code (250→250,
  not 200). This is the textbook opposite of weakening-to-go-green: the assertion tracks a real
  production fix, and the fix ENLARGES what's preserved (fewer rows dropped, not more).

**No-drop test is discriminating, not tautological:** input length 250 is deliberately > the old
200 cap, so a re-introduced `.slice(0,200)` regression yields 200≠250 → fails. Length-from-250-
distinct-inputs is the correct oracle for a "never drops rows" contract (any cap necessarily
shrinks length). Minor: it asserts only length, not that a specific low-vote row (e.g. id=0/
vote_average=0, the "newest un-voted" case the fix is ABOUT) survives — adding
`expect(out...cast.some(c => c.id === 0)).toBe(true)` would pin the user-facing intent more
directly, but length===250 already fully covers no-drop. The `vote_average: i` ascending fixture
shape is a harmless leftover from the old sort-proving cap test (irrelevant now — no sort exists).

**No coverage loss from dropping the cap test:** the capped/sorted behavior no longer exists in
production, so there is nothing left to cover. `personSeed.ts` has no `.sort`/`.slice`.

**Points 3-4 re-confirmed:** the other five tests (fat-field drop via `'vote_count' in c`
key-absence, TV display-field passthrough, malformed-credit `??` defaults, crew `job`, character,
identity passthrough `toBe(p)`) are byte-identical to the version whose two MEDIUM gaps I closed
in the prior entry — all strict matchers, no `.skip`/`.only`, none tautological. **Verdict: PASS.**

**Pattern: a strict→different-assertion change is a red flag ONLY when the test bends to match
buggy output. When the PRODUCTION code changed first (here: a review-driven fix that removed a
user-visible truncation) and the new assertion pins the corrected contract with a discriminating
fixture, it is a legitimate behavior-update — verify by (a) reading prod to confirm the old
behavior is genuinely GONE (no dead sort/cap), and (b) checking the new fixture would fail if the
old behavior were reintroduced (250>200 catches a re-added slice).**

**Update 2026-07-09 (re-review) — suggested targeting assertion ADDED, verified honest.** The
prior entry noted the no-drop test pinned only `length===250` and suggested
`expect(out...cast.some(c => c.id === 0)).toBe(true)` to pin the user-facing intent (the
newest un-voted row surviving). That exact line is now added. Verified: fixture builds 250
credits with `id: i` / `vote_average: i` ascending, so id=0 is the lowest-vote row — precisely
the one a `.sort(vote_average desc).slice(0,200)` cap would slice out FIRST. `.some(c=>c.id===0)`
is discriminating, not tautological: id=0 is a specific row among 250 distinct ids, present only
if that row survives; a re-added vote_average cap drops it (and would also break length===250, so
both oracles catch the regression, this one more directly names the intent). Confirmed prod
`personSeed.ts` still has no `.slice`/`.sort` (grep: only `vote_average ?? 0` passthrough default,
OBS comment lines 22-24 documents the cap removal). Nothing else in the diff changed vs. the
version I PASSED; no assertion weakened, no `.skip`/`.only`. **Verdict: PASS.** Pattern reinforced:
a "never drops rows" contract is fully covered by `length===N` (N > old cap), but adding a
`.some(id===specificLowRankRow)` assertion that names the EXACT row the removed cap sliced first
makes the regression's user-facing intent legible in the test — cheap, honest, worth keeping.

### 2026-07-16 — forward-revert of BIN-523/BIN-510 (sprint 84e7f4d → fd4b14e): reviewing a REVERT for test-honesty needs a different protocol than reviewing a change — export-delta + test-count arithmetic, not mutation-testing

**Context:** first revert-shaped diff I've reviewed. A deploy-RED sprint (`84e7f4d`, 7 tickets) backed
out 2 verification-failed tickets; BIN-523's `functions/src/availableNotify/logic.test.ts` was reverted
ALONGSIDE its code, which superficially looks exactly like the forbidden "delete tests to go green".
It isn't — but the distinction has to be PROVEN, not assumed. **Verdict: APPROVED.**

**The protocol that actually discriminates (reusable for any future revert):**
1. **Blob-hash the index against the revert target**, don't read the diff. `git rev-parse <target>:<path>`
   vs `git ls-files -s <path>` for every file → identical hashes prove genuine restoration and kill the
   "hand-edited/weakened variant smuggled in under a revert label" hypothesis in one shot. `git diff
   --cached <target> -- <paths>` being empty is the same proof in aggregate. Also diff worktree vs index
   (unstaged drift would ship something neither reviewed nor claimed).
2. **Export-delta, not line-diff, answers "did a test lose its subject".** `git show A:file | grep ^export`
   vs `git show B:file | grep ^export` → here exactly `NotifyMediaType`/`normalizeMediaType`/
   `availableStateDocId` vanished, and exactly the 2 describe blocks naming those 2 functions vanished.
   1:1 correspondence = tests died WITH their code. The inverse (a symbol surviving whose describe block
   disappeared) is the real red flag this check is FOR.
3. **Test-count arithmetic is the cheapest proof that nothing ELSE vanished silently.** File went 15 its
   → 12; suite went 1940 (the sprint commit's own claim, corroborated by the prior marker entry) → 1937.
   Δ=3 on both sides = exactly the 3 reverted tests, nothing else. **A revert's suite-count delta must
   equal the count of tests whose production code the revert also removes — any excess is a silently
   dropped test.** This one line of arithmetic is worth more than re-reading the whole diff.
4. **Module-private removals can't break tests — check the export surface before hunting importers.**
   BIN-510's `groups.ts` revert removed `MY_GROUPS_LIMIT`/`zeroGroupsCache`/`noteGroupMembership`/
   `knownZeroGroups` — all module-private, so no test COULD depend on them. The 2 retained tests that
   `vi.mock('@/lib/firebase/groups')` fully replace the module and never load the real file → immune by
   construction. Confirm no exported *signature* changed and you're done.
5. **Check the retained coverage/CI gates for interaction.** The same sprint added BIN-525's coverage
   step (retained). Had it carried `thresholds`, deleting tests could red-light CI and pressure someone
   into re-weakening. It didn't: `continue-on-error: true`, no thresholds, `include: ['src/**']` — so
   `functions/src` (where the reverted tests lived) isn't even in the denominator. **A revert landing
   into a repo that gained a coverage gate in the SAME commit is a real interaction to check, not
   hypothetical.**

**"Newly untested retained code" has a subtlety worth naming:** reverting code that shipped with ZERO
tests removes ZERO coverage. BIN-510's groups.ts additions were untested (the sprint itself filed
BIN-530 for the missing test), so the revert is coverage-neutral by definition. The question is never
"did tests disappear" but "did any surviving line lose its only oracle".

**Traceability side-finding (extends the 2026-07-09 BIN-440 marker-hygiene lesson to TICKETS):** a
revert orphans the follow-up tickets filed against the reverted code. BIN-530 ("missing MY_GROUPS_LIMIT
bounded-query test") now owes a test for a constant that no longer exists; BIN-529 ("inbox doc id STILL
bare tmdbId") was worded against the post-BIN-523 world and reads as false once everything is bare
tmdbId again. **When reviewing a revert, read the reverted commit's own "known follow-ups" list and flag
the ones the revert invalidates** — otherwise a future sprint writes a test for deleted code. Cheap,
and nobody else in the pipeline is looking at it.

**Also worth knowing for a BIN-523 re-attempt:** the 3 deleted pure-helper tests were the ONLY coverage
that area ever had — `availableNotify/index.ts` imports firebase-admin, has no test file, so the
grouping/doc-id WIRING was untested in both versions (classic instance of the "extract the pure helper,
leave the wiring uncovered" gap). And the revert target `fd4b14e` is what's LIVE, so a revert to it
restores parity with production rather than introducing risk — worth stating explicitly in the verdict,
because "this revert reintroduces a known bug" sounds alarming until you note production never left it.

### 2026-07-17 — BIN-510 retry (groups.ts zero-groups cache): a cache-invalidation test that never PRIMES the cache first is non-discriminating for its own claim

**Context:** reviewed `src/lib/firebase/groups.ts` + new `groups.test.ts` (BIN-510 zero-groups
cache retry + BIN-532 atomic-batch createGroup/addToGroupWatchlist). Most of the file is
solid: `createGroup`'s atomic-batch test proves ordering via ref-path binding
(`setMock.mock.calls[0][0]` group doc, `[1][0]` member doc, same auto-id), `addToGroupWatchlist`'s
merge:true test asserts `payload` lacks `memberRatings` via `not.toHaveProperty` (real
key-absence, not a stub), and most of the BIN-510 zero-groups cache tests correctly PRIME the
cache first (e.g. "createGroup ogiltigförklarar…" calls `syncProgressToGroups` with an empty
scan first to seed the known-empty cache, THEN calls `createGroup`, THEN proves a real scan
happens again).

**One test breaks that pattern and is vacuous as a result: "removeMember stör inte ett
efterföljande riktigt scan-resultat" (`groups.test.ts:321-329`).** It calls `removeMember('g1',
'me')` directly on a FRESH module (uid 'me' was never marked known-empty), then asserts a
subsequent `syncProgressToGroups` does a real scan. Mutation-tested live on the real prod file
(deleted `invalidateGroupsCache(uid)` from `removeMember`, `groups.ts:317` — ran the full 13-test
suite, restored, confirmed `git diff` byte-identical after): **all 13 tests stayed green**,
including this one. The reason: `isKnownGroupsEmpty('me')` is `false` whether or not
`removeMember` calls `invalidateGroupsCache` at all, because nothing in the test ever made it
`true` first. **Pattern (new instance, generalizes the existing "gate fixture must fail every
OTHER condition" mutation-testing lesson to invalidation-style functions): a test for "X
invalidates a cache" must first PUT something in the cache for X to invalidate — proving "the
cache is still empty after X" when it started empty proves nothing about X.** Same failure mode
as the 2026-07-16 BIN-513 compound-guard entry (a guard test that doesn't isolate its own
guard), just on a stateful cache instead of a sequential predicate. Fix: prime via
`subscribeToMyGroups` `onNext(emptySnap())` or a `syncProgressToGroups` empty-scan call before
`removeMember`, matching the already-correct sibling tests in the same describe block.

### 2026-07-18 — BIN-543 same-day follow-up: moving MAX_PAGES's export from a firebase-functions-importing file into the already-extracted admin-free config.ts is a CI unbreak, not a weakening

**Context:** the earlier same-day BIN-543 entry (below, timestamped 07:30:17Z in the marker) closed
a MEDIUM by moving `CADENCE_HOURS`/`LEAVING_HARD_CYCLE_CAP` into a new admin-free `./config.ts` so
`motnChanges.test.ts` could live-import them instead of hand-duplicating literals. This immediate
follow-up discovered that `MAX_PAGES` itself — still `export`ed from `motnChanges.ts`, which imports
`logger` from `'firebase-functions/v2'` — resolves fine locally (dev `node_modules` has the package)
but fails under CI's fresh `npm ci` (root vitest toolchain doesn't install `firebase-functions`, same
"Functions test import gotcha" class as the pre-existing firebase-admin one, just a different package).
Fix: move `MAX_PAGES`'s *definition* into the same `./config.ts` (not just re-export it from there —
actually relocate), `motnChanges.ts` now imports it back for its own runtime use (the `for (let page
= 0; page < MAX_PAGES; page++)` loop).

**Verified this is a pure CI-unbreak, not a red flag:** (1) grepped every `MAX_PAGES` reference in
`functions/src` — value is still `18`, single definition, and `index.ts`/`motnChanges.ts` both import
the *same* three constants from the *same* `./config.ts` the test now imports from, so there's no
diverged/stale copy anywhere production reads from vs. what the test reads from. (2) The test's
assertion logic is byte-for-byte identical to the prior commit — `git diff --cached` shows only the
import line changed (`import { MAX_PAGES } from './motnChanges'` + `import {
LEAVING_HARD_CYCLE_CAP, CADENCE_HOURS } from './config'` → one combined `import { MAX_PAGES,
LEAVING_HARD_CYCLE_CAP, CADENCE_HOURS } from './config'`). (3) Ran the test live: 1/1 pass, still
proves the real arithmetic (`runsPerCycle===8`, `18*8=144<=150`) against production constants.

**Pattern (generalizes the "Functions test import gotcha" reference beyond firebase-admin): ANY
`firebase-functions/*` import in a file also makes that file's exports untestable from root CI, not
just `firebase-admin` imports.** When a pure constant/helper needs to be test-imported and its home
file imports from `firebase-functions/v2` (schedulers, logger, secrets, etc.), the fix is the same
"extract to an admin/functions-free `config.ts`/`logic.ts`" pattern already established — check for
BOTH import families before declaring a helper file safe to import from a root-vitest test. **Verdict:
APPROVED**, no weakening — moving a constant's home module while keeping its value and every
consumer's source-of-truth identical is refactor-grade, not test-grade, and here it demonstrably fixes
a real CI break rather than papering over one.

### 2026-07-18 — BIN-544 recapCoverage `validateMissInput`: 8/8 discriminating (mentally mutation-traced), but "non-object payload" test has non-discriminating sub-cases + two real untested numeric edges

**Context:** new file, `functions/src/recapCoverage/logic.test.ts` against `logic.ts`'s
`validateMissInput(raw)` — a callable-input validator (`!raw || typeof raw !== 'object'` guard,
then `Number(data.tmdbId)` coerce + `Number.isInteger(tmdbId) && tmdbId > 0`). Traced every
assertion by hand against the guard clauses (no live mutation edit needed — the function is 6
lines, hand-tracing each fixture through each branch is exact here). All 8 `it()` blocks proved
genuinely falsifiable against the specific guard they name, EXCEPT one sub-case documented below.
Confirmed `index.ts`'s only consumer never reads anything off `request.data` except through
`parsed.value.tmdbId` (doc id = `String(...)`, write body = `{count, lastMissedAt}` only) — so the
"ignores extra fields" test is real defense-in-depth, not theater. 8/8 pass live.

**Non-discriminating sub-case (LOW, informational, not blocking): the "rejects a non-object
payload" test's `'603'` and `603` fixtures don't actually exercise `typeof raw !== 'object'`.**
Hand-traced: delete that guard clause entirely (keep only `!raw`) → `null` still gets caught
(and would otherwise CRASH — `null.tmdbId` throws — so the null fixture is the one genuinely
load-bearing case, catching the mutation via an uncaught exception rather than a false
assertion). But `'603'.tmdbId` and `(603).tmdbId` are just `undefined` on a primitive (no
throw), which falls through to `Number(undefined) → NaN → Number.isInteger(NaN) === false` and
gets rejected anyway — same outcome with or without the guard clause. **This is structurally
different from the usual "gate fixture must fail every OTHER condition" finding (BIN-513/BIN-510
entries above): here there is no possible non-null, non-undefined fixture that WOULD
discriminate this specific guard clause, because JS property access on any primitive silently
returns `undefined` rather than throwing.** Worth naming so a future reader doesn't assume all 3
sub-assertions independently prove 3 things — only 1 does; the other 2 duplicate the "rejects a
missing tmdbId" test's NaN path under a different label. Not asking for a fix (there isn't a
better fixture); asking that reviewers recognize this shape (type-guard whose non-crash branches
are unreachable-by-design) as a case where "counted assertions" overstate real coverage.

**Two genuine, unraised production/test gaps (both LOW-MEDIUM, non-blocking, worth a follow-up):**
1. **No upper bound / no `Number.isSafeInteger`.** `Number.isInteger(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1)`
   is `true` in JS (it only checks for a fractional part, not safe-integer range), so an
   arbitrarily large `tmdbId` passes today. Past `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, distinct raw inputs can
   collide onto the same IEEE-754 float (e.g. two adjacent huge integers round to the same
   value), letting one caller's `logRecapMiss` land on a doc id the caller didn't actually send.
   No test pins this either direction. Fix candidates: gate on `Number.isSafeInteger` instead of
   `Number.isInteger`, and/or cap to a realistic TMDB-id ceiling (current catalog tops out well
   under 10 million).
2. **Boolean coercion silently accepted.** `{tmdbId: true}` → `Number(true) === 1` →
   `Number.isInteger(1) && 1 > 0` → **accepted** as `tmdbId: 1`. (`{tmdbId: false}` is rejected,
   but only because `Number(false) === 0` fails the `<= 0` check, not because booleans are
   rejected as a type.) No test exercises a boolean fixture. Given the module docstring's stated
   contract ("validated as a positive integer"), a boolean silently becoming a real integer is
   surprising leniency in the same family as the already-tested `'not-a-number'` string case —
   add `expect(validateMissInput({ tmdbId: true }).ok).toBe(false)` and, if the intent is to
   close this for real, gate the coercion behind `typeof data.tmdbId === 'number' ||
   typeof data.tmdbId === 'string'` before calling `Number(...)`.

**Float `603.0` explicitly checked and confirmed a non-issue:** JS has no separate int/float
runtime type (`603.0 === 603`), so there is nothing distinguishable to test beyond the existing
"accepts a valid positive integer tmdbId" case — not a gap, just verifying the prompt's specific
question rather than leaving it open.

**Verdict: CONDITIONAL PASS.** No weakened/deleted/skipped assertions, nothing tautological in
the blocking sense; the 2 numeric-edge gaps and 1 non-discriminating sub-case pair are real but
narrow (an internal counter doc, not an access-control or user-data surface) — filed as follow-up
test-hardening notes, not a block on this commit.

**Additional coverage gaps (absence, not weakening) named for the calling agent, not written up
further here since they don't establish a new pattern beyond "extract the pure helper, leave the
fan-out wiring uncovered" (2026-07-09 BIN-440 entry) applied to a Firestore module instead of a
`functions/` I/O file:** `deleteGroup` (the file's most complex fan-out — chunked batch,
household-uid derivation, orphaned-session cleanup, and its own `invalidateGroupsCache` call) has
zero test coverage; `joinGroupViaToken`/`acceptGroupInvite`'s cache-invalidate-on-success calls
are untested; `refreshMyHouseholdContributions`'s dirty-check skip-write path is untested (the
mock hardcodes `contributionContentEquals: () => false`, so the "no write when unchanged"
cost-cap-relevant contract is never exercised in either direction); `getRecentSessionPicksAcrossGroups`'s
actual multi-group merge/sort/slice fan-out logic is untested beyond the bounded-`limit()`
empty-snapshot case.

**Verdict: CHANGES REQUESTED** (test-quality gap + coverage gaps, not a red-flag weakening — no
assertion was deleted, loosened, or rewritten to match buggy output anywhere in the diff).

### 2026-07-16 — BIN-509 rules tests (participants slot-hijack + swipes vote-binding): 2 of 3 load-bearing clauses cleanly test-locked, one named "shape gate" test is non-discriminating for its own guard because a SIBLING guard (get()-on-missing-doc) already covers the fixture

**Context:** reviewed `src/test/rules/firestore-rules.test.ts` working-tree diff (BIN-24 fixture
contract update to token-shaped ids + new `sessions/{id}/participants` slot-hijack/pre-plant block
+ new `sessions/{id}/swipes` vote-binding block) against `firestore.rules`. Mutation-tested 3
clauses on the real rules file (each restored + md5-confirmed byte-identical before the next):
(1) the signed-in own-key `affectedKeys().hasOnly([auth.uid])` bind on swipes update, (2) the
`anonShapedPid(pid)` gate in the participants anon-branch OR-clause, (3) the
`changedKeys()/removedKeys()==0` add-only guard in `anonVoteAddOk()`. Each flipped EXACTLY 1 test,
the one whose name matches the mutated clause — clean 1:1 test-lock for all 3.

**The gap (MEDIUM, non-blocking): two tests both claim to cover the `anonShapedPid()` shape gate on
different surfaces (participants create-path vs. swipes vote-key), but only ONE actually does.**
`voteKeyIsAnonSlot(k) = anonShapedPid(k) && get(.../participants/$(k)).data.uid == null` is used on
BOTH the swipes create and update branches. The test "a uid-shaped (non-token) vote key is denied
by the shape gate — the pre-plant swipe leg" votes under key `'victim_real_uid'`, for which NO
participant doc was ever seeded. Removing ONLY `anonShapedPid(k)` from `voteKeyIsAnonSlot` (leaving
the `get()` call) and rerunning: 193/193 still green — the test passes because `get()` on a
never-existing doc denies via the missing-doc error path, the IDENTICAL mechanism the sibling test
"a token-shaped vote key with no participant doc behind it is denied (get() denies)" already
covers. The test name promises proof of the shape gate; the fixture actually proves the
missing-doc gate. Contrast: the analogous PARTICIPANTS-side pre-plant test ("anon caller cannot
PRE-PLANT a ghost slot at a real uid's path") genuinely flips when `anonShapedPid(pid)` is removed
from the *participants* rule, because there `resource == null` alone doesn't deny (the anon branch
has no `get()` fallback) — same shape-gate INTENT, different surrounding guards, only one actually
isolates it.

**Pattern (extends the "gate fixture true on every OTHER condition" principle from the extracted-
predicates section, and the 2026-07-16 BIN-513 mediaType-guard entry above): when the SAME named
guard (here `anonShapedPid`) is reused across two call sites that have DIFFERENT sibling guards
(participants: only the shape check stands between the fixture and allow; swipes: a `get()`
missing-doc error ALSO denies the same fixture independently), a test written against one call site
does not transfer to the other — each call site needs its own mutation-verified fixture. The
diagnostic is the same as always: delete only the guard under test (not its neighbors), rerun, and
check that ONLY the intended test flips. A fixture that "looks like" it targets a shape gate because
the id is uid-shaped is not proof unless every other path to denial (missing doc, wrong branch,
absent participant) is independently ruled out for that specific surface.** Not currently
exploitable (the participants-side gate already prevents a uid-shaped anon slot from ever being
created via client writes, so there's no reachable state where the swipes-side shape check alone
would matter) — filed as a test-hardening note, not a blocker.

**No weakening found in the diff**: BIN-24 fixture rewrite (`p1`/`anon1` → `OWNER`/32-hex token
constants) is a legitimate contract-TIGHTENING (adds `pid == auth.uid` path binding on top of the
existing uid-field check; new fixtures are strictly more constrained, matching real

### 2026-07-10 — BIN-402 tmdbFieldsSweep: new-field-on-a-hasOnly()-doc without a rules update is a live "next client write breaks" bug, not a "future refresh button" nice-to-have

**Context:** `functions/src/tmdbTosSweep/{logic.ts,logic.test.ts,index.ts}` (all new) + a
re-export line in `functions/src/index.ts`. All 15 `logic.test.ts` tests are honest and
thorough — boundary tests on `isTmdbFieldsStale` (exact 5-month edge kept, +1ms/-1ms both
directions), `allTargetFieldsAbsent` correctly treats explicit-null/empty-array as "present"
(not absent), and `buildClearedPayload`'s key-set is asserted set-equal to
`TMDB_DERIVED_FIELDS ∪ {tmdbFieldsRefreshedAt}` plus a disjointness check against
`FORBIDDEN_FIELDS` — and cross-checking both arrays against the real `WatchlistItem` type
(`src/types/domain.ts:31-86`) shows every field is accounted for in exactly one of the two
lists (no silent carve-out). Ran the suite: 15/15 green. `index.ts` (firebase-admin-importing
entrypoint) is correctly left untested, matching the sibling `retentionCleanup`/
`episodeNotify` convention (only `logic.ts` gets a root-vitest test; admin-importing code
never does).

**The real gap is not in the test file — it's the rules file this diff DIDN'T touch.**
`firestore.rules`'s `isValidWatchlistItem()` (`firestore.rules:91-131`) still `hasOnly([...])`s
the pre-existing field list and has NOT been given a `tmdbFieldsRefreshedAt` entry. ADR 0009
lists this as a plain "Consequences" bullet ("added to `firestore.rules` `hasOnly()`
whitelist") but the plan doc's own "Kärnbeslut" section frames the risk as protecting only
"en framtida klient-refreshknapp" (a hypothetical future client refresh button) — **that
framing undersells the actual blast radius.** `WatchlistContext`'s existing, everyday write
paths (`updateRating`, `updateStatus`, `setNotes`, `setRuntime`, `updateProgress`,
`setTmdbStatus`, `nextAirReadRepair.flushNextAirWrites`, ...) all call
`setDoc(ref, {...partial}, { merge: true })` — and Firestore rules evaluate
`request.resource.data` for a merge-write as the FULL POST-MERGE document (confirmed against
this repo's own 2026-07-02 next-air-read-repair entry above: "rules accept-tests correctly
use `{ merge: true }`... merge-post-doc otherwise passes hasOnly"). So the instant
`mutateEnabled` flips true and the sweep stamps `tmdbFieldsRefreshedAt` on a real doc, the
VERY NEXT ordinary client action on that SAME doc (rate a movie, mark an episode watched,
add a tag) re-evaluates `isValidWatchlistItem` against a document that now includes an
unlisted key → `hasOnly()` fails → `permission-denied` on a completely unrelated user action.
This is TODAY's write path, not a future one — the plan's risk note is simply wrong about
scope, and no test anywhere (root or `vitest.rules.config.ts`) exercises "client merge-writes
to a doc the sweep has already stamped," so nothing currently catches it.

**Recommendation:** before `sweepState/tmdbFieldsSweep.mutateEnabled` is ever flipped to
`true` in prod, `firestore.rules` MUST add `'tmdbFieldsRefreshedAt'` to
`isValidWatchlistItem`'s `hasOnly()` list (+ a nullable-timestamp type bind, mirroring
`ratedAt`/`nextAirUpdatedAt`) and ship with a new `vitest.rules.config.ts` regression test:
seed a watchlist doc WITH `tmdbFieldsRefreshedAt` already set (simulating a post-sweep doc),
then `assertSucceeds` on an ordinary owner merge-write (e.g. a rating change) that doesn't
touch that field. Without that test, this exact regression class (new server-stamped field on
a `hasOnly()`-gated doc, forgotten in the client whitelist) will keep recurring — this is the
project's second confirmed instance of "merge-post-doc must pass hasOnly" being the load-
bearing rules mechanic (first: `ratedAt`/`nextAir*` fields, both correctly whitelisted when
introduced). **Pattern: any new field a Cloud Function (Admin SDK, rules-exempt) starts
writing onto a `hasOnly()`-gated, client-writable doc needs the SAME-COMMIT (or explicitly
gated, pre-flip) rules whitelist update — Admin SDK bypassing rules protects the writer, never
the doc's future client-side readers/writers.**

**Verdict: test file itself is APPROVED (honest, thorough, no weakening) — but flag the
missing companion `firestore.rules` change as a blocking pre-flip item, not a "someday" one.**

### 2026-07-11 — BIN-360 releaseNotify: revert of a Stockholm-timezone over-correction, verified by actually computing the counterfactual, not just reading prose

**Context:** second review pass on `functions/src/releaseNotify/logic.test.ts` (first pass
approved a version that converted `seDigitalReleaseDates` through `stockholmDateString`; that
production code was then reverted back to a plain `slice(0, 10)` of TMDB's stated date, because
TMDB type-4 dates are calendar dates, not instants — converting them through a timezone could
roll a `22:00Z` entry forward to the next day, which is wrong). Two tests changed to match: the
renamed "uses the STATED calendar date, not a timezone-shifted instant" test (asserts
`2026-07-11T22:00:00.000Z` → `['2026-07-11']`) and the malformed-date test (now `'2026'`, a
4-char string that fails the `length >= 10` guard, → `[]`).

**Did not just trust the test's own comment — computed the counterfactual directly.** Read
`functions/src/releaseNotify/logic.ts` and confirmed the live code is `rd.release_date.slice(0,
10)` (no timezone math at all) with a `length >= 10` guard before the slice. Then ran the actual
Stockholm conversion the removed code would have used
(`Intl.DateTimeFormat('sv-SE', { timeZone: 'Europe/Stockholm', ... }).format(new
Date('2026-07-11T22:00:00.000Z'))`) via `node -e`: it returns `'2026-07-12'` (Sweden is UTC+2 in
July/CEST) — which would NOT equal the test's expected `['2026-07-11']`. So the changed
assertion is a genuine two-sided oracle: it demonstrably fails against the just-removed
timezone-conversion code and passes against the reverted `slice`-based code, exactly the
"strengthening, not weakening" bar this file requires. This is the same discipline as the
2026-07-09 xhigh-verification entries above — re-derive the counterfactual from the actual
algorithm, don't just accept a comment's claim that it would fail.

The `stockholmDateString` DST tests (fall-back anchor, per `reference_dst_test_anchor`) are
byte-identical — correct, since that function still exists and is still used by the caller to
compute "today" (the boundary that genuinely needs a timezone, per the file's own docstring
distinguishing "stated release date" from "current Swedish calendar day"). Ran the file: 13/13
pass. **Pattern for future date/timezone reverts:** when a test's justification hinges on "this
would fail against the old code," don't take that on faith — compute the old code's actual
output for the same input and confirm the assertion really does discriminate.

**Verdict: APPROVED.** Assertions changed in lockstep with a real, verified production revert;
not a weakening.

### 2026-07-11 — BIN-402 re-review: the missing `firestore.rules` companion flagged 2026-07-10 is now shipped, tests genuinely close the gap

**Context:** follow-up to the 2026-07-10 entry above ("new-field-on-a-hasOnly()-doc without a
rules update is a live bug"). This staged diff adds exactly what was recommended: `firestore.rules`
`isValidWatchlistItem()` now whitelists `'tmdbFieldsRefreshedAt'` in `hasOnly()` plus a type bind
`(d.tmdbFieldsRefreshedAt is timestamp && d.tmdbFieldsRefreshedAt <= request.time)` — the
`<= request.time` half is new hardening beyond what was asked (blocks a client from writing a
FUTURE stamp to make the sweep perpetually treat the doc as fresh, i.e. neuter the ToS clear).
Four new `firestore-rules.test.ts` tests: (1) seeds a post-sweep doc (`tmdbFieldsRefreshedAt` already
set) then asserts an ordinary owner merge-write (rating change) still succeeds — this is the EXACT
regression class the 2026-07-10 entry named; (2) a bare stamp merge-write succeeds; (3) a
non-timestamp value is rejected (type bind); (4) a `Timestamp.fromMillis(Date.now() + 24h)` value
is rejected (the `<=request.time` bind).

**Verified test 4 is a genuine oracle, not incidental.** Attempted a live mutation (temporarily
dropped the `&& d.tmdbFieldsRefreshedAt <= request.time` clause down to a bare `is timestamp`
check) to re-run `npm run test:rules` against the weakened rule — the harness's own auto-mode
classifier denied that Bash call outright ("[Security Weaken]... a security hardening the user
asked to verify, not delete; weakening it was not authorized"), which is itself a useful guardrail
signal (it correctly recognized a firestore.rules edit that strips a security bind, even as a
throwaway local mutation for verification purposes) — reverted the file immediately, confirmed
`git diff --stat` empty. Fell back to direct rule-construction analysis instead: the tomorrow-
`Timestamp` fixture is a real `Timestamp` object, so it passes `is timestamp` unconditionally;
`<= request.time` is the ONLY clause in the disjunction that a future value can fail, so removing
it flips `assertFails` to `assertSucceeds` and the test would fail — logically airtight without
needing the live run. **Lesson for future mutation-testing of firestore.rules specifically: the
permission classifier will block a Bash call that runs tests against an in-place-weakened
firestore.rules, even mid-review with immediate revert planned — verify these by inspection/
reasoning instead of live mutation, or ask the user first if a live mutation run is essential.**

Ran both the root suite and the rules suite for real (unmutated) state: `npx vitest run

### 2026-07-11 — BIN-402 second re-review: `buildClearedPayload` arity change + a stamp-exclusion revert in `nextAirReadRepair.test.ts` — both correctly track a same-session production correction, not weakening

**Context:** shipping dry-run gate, same HEAD (3af9a85) as the two entries directly above.
Two production edits landed after the prior APPROVAL and the parent agent specifically asked me
to distinguish "assertion changed to match a real fix" from "assertion loosened to dodge a bug."

**`buildClearedPayload`: 2-arg → 1-arg (`deleteSentinel` only), and now deletes the freshness
stamp too (was: set it to `serverTimestamp()`).** Read `logic.ts`'s new docstring (lines 117-131):
the old set-fresh behavior was itself the bug — leaving `tmdbFieldsRefreshedAt` freshly stamped on
a doc whose TMDB fields were just cleared would make `needsTmdbFieldsRefresh` return `false`, so
the swept doc renders blank (title/poster/providers gone) until the stamp aged out ~90 days on its
own — i.e. the ToS-clear and the lazy-repopulate mechanism would fight each other for months. The
fix is to delete the stamp alongside every derived field, so the doc ends fully absent-stamped and
the very next title-page view's `needsTmdbFieldsRefresh(null, now) === true` repopulates it
immediately. Checked `index.ts`'s call site (line 142): `buildClearedPayload(FieldValue.delete())`
— single delete sentinel reused for the whole payload, consistent with the new one-arg signature
(the old signature presumably took a second `freshSentinel` arg for the now-removed `serverTimestamp()`
branch). Verified the test file matches exactly: `key set is EXACTLY... plus the freshness stamp`
(exact-set-equality against `[...TMDB_DERIVED_FIELDS, TMDB_FIELDS_STAMP].sort()`, unchanged),
`every clearable field maps to the delete sentinel` (unchanged), a NEW test `'DELETES the freshness
stamp too'` asserting `payload[TMDB_FIELDS_STAMP]).toBe(DELETE)` (replaces what would have been a
`toBe(FRESH_SENTINEL)`-style assertion under the old behavior — this is the correct direction: the
test now pins the corrected behavior, and would fail against the old buggy set-fresh code), and the
`FORBIDDEN_FIELDS`/`updatedAt` guard block is byte-identical to the 2026-07-10-reviewed version.
This is a genuine strengthening: the test discriminates the fix from the bug it replaces, not a
loosening to accommodate broken output.

**`nextAirReadRepair.test.ts`: `buildRepairPayload`'s key-set assertion reverted from 4 keys back
to 3 (drops `tmdbFieldsRefreshedAt`), plus a new explicit `'tmdbFieldsRefreshedAt' in payload ===
false` line.** This is the mirror-image correction on the OTHER writer. The 2026-07-11 entry above
(same file, prior state) had approved a version where the subset-only `nextAirReadRepair` writer
ALSO stamped the whole-block freshness field — but `nextAirReadRepair.ts`'s own updated docstring
(lines 61-69) now explains why that was wrong: it only writes `nextAirDate`/`nextAirCode`/
`nextAirProvider`, never `title`/`posterPath`/`providers`/etc., so stamping the doc-level "whole
TMDB block is fresh" marker from a partial write would be dishonest — a calendar-active user who
never opens a title page would show `title`/`providers` as perpetually fresh (never re-fetched) and
the sweep would never touch them, silently defeating the §1.C compliance mechanism this whole
feature exists for. Confirmed `buildRepairPayload` itself no longer includes the stamp key (just
`{...delta, nextAirUpdatedAt: stamp}` — grep-verified, no `tmdbFieldsRefreshedAt` reference in the
production file at all now) and that `WatchlistContext.refreshTmdbFields` (the full-block title-page
writer) is the one now carrying `tmdbFieldsRefreshedAt: serverTimestamp()`, alongside `addItem`
(both verified directly in the `WatchlistContext.tsx` diff). So the test correction traces exactly
to which writer legitimately owns the stamp — full-block writers (`addItem`, `refreshTmdbFields`)
stamp it; the partial writer (`nextAirReadRepair`) does not. The load-bearing `'updatedAt' in
payload === false` guard is untouched. This is the same "assertion count went down but for a real,
traceable reason" pattern as the 2026-07-03 `campaignPricing` entries — never accept a shrinking
key-set assertion without reading the corresponding production diff to confirm the removed key
really did leave the payload, not just the test.

Ran all three assigned files together: `npx vitest run functions/src/tmdbTosSweep/logic.test.ts
src/lib/watchlist/nextAirReadRepair.test.ts src/lib/watchlist/tmdbFieldsRefresh.test.ts` → 29/29
green (unchanged count from the entry above — `tmdbFieldsRefresh.test.ts`'s gate logic is
untouched by either of these two production edits, confirmed by diff: no changes to that file or
its `.ts` counterpart in this pass).

**Verdict: APPROVED.** Both edits are corrections that follow real, cross-checked production fixes
(verified against `logic.ts`'s docstring + `index.ts`'s call site, and `nextAirReadRepair.ts`'s
docstring + `WatchlistContext.tsx`'s diff respectively) — not weakenings. `firestore.rules`'
`tmdbFieldsRefreshedAt` whitelist + `<= request.time` bind (reviewed 2026-07-11 above) is

### 2026-07-11 — BIN-463/464 releaseNotify cache + catch-up window: genuine new oracles, but the Firestore-doc-parse step still isn't pure-extracted

**Context:** `functions/src/releaseNotify/logic.ts` gains a per-title release-date cache
(`shouldRefetchReleaseDates`, TTL-gated) and a catch-up/grace-window + per-user dedup marker
(`isWithinFireWindow`, `releaseDateToFire`, `shouldNotifyRelease`) on top of the already-shipped
BIN-360 "släpps idag" push. `logic.test.ts`'s diff is entirely additive — the pre-existing
`seDigitalReleaseDates`/`releasesDigitallyToday`/`stockholmDateString` tests are byte-identical
(confirmed via `git diff`), no `.skip`, nothing removed or loosened.

**Genuine oracles confirmed:** `isWithinFireWindow` pins BOTH sides of the grace-day boundary
(`+3`→true, `+4`→false) and the release-day boundary (`0`→true, `-1`→false) — the full
must-have set. `releaseDateToFire`'s "prefers the LATEST in-window date" fixture lists the
earlier date FIRST (`['2026-07-11','2026-07-13']`) so a first-wins regression (`if(best===null)
best=d`) would return the wrong (earlier) date and fail — correct fixture-ordering discipline.
`shouldNotifyRelease`'s 3 cases (no-marker, same-date-suppress, newer-date-re-arms) are a clean
inequality oracle. The `RELEASE_CATCHUP_GRACE_DAYS >= RELEASE_REFETCH_TTL_DAYS` test asserts the
actual exported constants against each other (not hardcoded numbers) — pins a real design
invariant that can never silently drift.

**Gap 1 (medium) — the Firestore-doc→`ReleaseDateCache` parse step lives in the
firebase-admin-importing file and has ZERO test coverage.** `readReleaseCache`
(`functions/src/availableNotify/index.ts:75-85`) does non-trivial parsing — `Array.isArray`
+ per-element `typeof === 'string'` filtering on `seDigitalDates`, and a `ts && typeof
ts.toMillis === 'function' ? ts.toMillis() : null` guard on the Timestamp field — but because
it's in the same file as `getFirestore()`, root vitest can't reach it and there's no
functions-emulator test either. This is exactly the shape of logic the codebase's own
extraction convention exists for (BIN-350 `dayId.ts`, BIN-326 `rollup.helpers.ts`): pull it
into `releaseNotify/logic.ts` as a pure `parseReleaseDateCache(raw: unknown): ReleaseDateCache`
taking a plain object (a `{ toMillis: () => N }` fake needs no firebase-admin import) and test
the array-filter guard and the timestamp-shape guard directly. As shipped, a dropped
`Array.isArray` check or a typo'd `toMillis` guard would be invisible to any test.

**Gap 2 (low) — exact TTL boundary (`ageMs === ttlDays*MS_PER_DAY`) untested from either side.**
The "refetches once older than TTL" test uses an age of `TTL_DAYS*DAY + DAY` (well past), and
the "trusts a fresh cache" tests use 1-day-old caches (well within, TTL=2). Same "boundary
approached but not pinned exactly" class already flagged twice this week (priceChartGeometry
2026-07-04, tmdbFieldsRefresh 2026-07-11) — a `>=` → `>` regression at exactly the TTL would
slip through silently. Add `datesResolvedAtMs: now - ttlDays*DAY` (exact, expect true) +
`+1ms inside` (expect false).

**Gap 3 (low) — default-parameter path never exercised.** Both `shouldRefetchReleaseDates`'s
`opts` and `releaseDateToFire`'s `graceDays` are always passed explicitly in tests (matching the
current constants), never omitted — the real call sites in `runReleasePhase` DO omit them and
rely on the defaults. Values happen to coincide so behavior is currently proven either way, but
a broken default-argument wiring (e.g. a typo'd default object) wouldn't be caught by these
tests specifically. Low priority since it's `logic.ts`'s own default value being tested against
itself either way.

**Verdict: APPROVED-WITH-NOTES.** No weakening. Three non-blocking gaps (one medium: extract +
test the doc-parse step; two low: exact-TTL boundary, untested default-arg path) — recommend on
next touch, none block this commit. `firestore.rules` unaffected (correctly — `releaseNotifyState`
is Admin-SDK-only, never read by client rules, confirmed via grep of both `firestore.rules` and
`firestore.indexes.json` — no query against the collection either, so no composite index is
needed, consistent with the file's own "Admin SDK bypasses firestore.rules" comment).
